SG ELECTION 2026

Rodrigues Birkett and Otunnu Show Biggest Gains in UN SecGen Poll

  • Damilola Banjo
  • • August 21, 2026
1m read
  • Damilola Banjo
  • August 21, 2026
LEAVE A COMMENT
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:48
Instaread

Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana moved into first place in the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general among eight candidates so far, after the Security Council held its second secret straw poll, on Friday, Aug. 21. Uganda’s Olara Otunnu gained the sharpest percentage increase support for his candidacy. Yet no nominee drew the required nine yes votes from the Council poll to fully command a lead (see chart below).

Rodrigues Birkett received eight “encourage,” three “discourage” and four “no opinion” ballots, putting her narrowly ahead of Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan. Grynspan got seven encourage, four discourage and four no opinion. She led the first round of straw polls, held July 30, with 10 encourage, 1 discourage and 4 no opinion.

Rafael Grossi of Argentina also received seven encourage votes on Aug. 21, but six discourage and two no opinion. Macky Sall of Senegal recorded six encourage votes, seven discourage and two no opinion.

Olara Otunnu of Uganda drew five encourage votes, five discourage and five no opinion.

María Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador (nominated by Antigua and Barbuda) received four encourage votes, three discourage and eight no opinion.

Michelle Bachelet of Chile (nominated by Brazil and Mexico) drew just two encourage votes, six discourage and seven no opinion.

Ivonne A-Baki of Ecuador (nominated by Tonga), who joined the race after the first poll was held, received no encourage votes, eight discourage and seven no opinion.

Surprising results

Otunnu’s outcome reflected one of the clearest shifts from the July round of informal voting. As a relative latecomer to the race, who held his interactive dialogue with the General Assembly on Aug. 20, as part of the selection process, he more than doubled his encourage votes (from two to five). Some of the eight original no-opinion ballots he drew in July flipped into support in the second polling.


He still fell short of nine yes votes, the minimal tally required for any candidate to clinch the top UN leadership position under Article 27 of the UN Charter (not including a veto, which is not cast in the straw polls). A substantive Council decision requires nine affirmative votes, including the concurrence of the permanent members.

“It is no surprise that some of the candidates have gained or lost ground, particularly as the P5 begin to express their preferences more openly,” said Daniel Forti, the head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group think tank, referring to the five permanent members (Britain, China, France, Russia and US).

“No candidate has commanded a significant majority of Council members after two polls, which may convince others potential candidates that they now have an opportunity to jump into the race.”

A-Baki’s first appearance on the Council ballot produced the most unfavorable results of the round, with no member encouraging her candidacy and more than half voting to discourage it. Bachelet experienced the steepest decline in outright support, falling from six encourage votes in July to two on Aug. 21.

The vote on Friday morning, held in the Council’s private consultations room, was the second in a series that could stretch into the final months of the year before the 15-nation body recommends a single candidate to the General Assembly for final approval. The 193 members formally appoint the next secretary-general technically by Dec. 31, when António Guterres’s second term ends.

Speaking to reporters after the straw poll, Ambassador Christina Markus Lassen of Denmark, who holds the monthly rotating Council presidency, kept her remarks brief. “The second round of straw polls has taken place,” she said. “The candidates will be informed of the results through the respective permanent representatives of nominating member states.”

She added that the president of the General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, would also be notified that the poll had concluded. Asked when the next straw poll would take place, Lassen did not offer a date. Council members will eventually move to color-coded ballots, which can help to reveal vetoes.

Straw poll comparisons

Besides Grynspan, who ceded her first place spot to Rodrigues Birkett in the Aug. 21 ballot, Grossi held steady on encourage votes but opposition to his candidacy tripled, from two discourage votes to six. Bachelet’s support collapsed, falling from six encourage votes to two. Sall’s tally was unchanged from the first round. No Council member indicated support for A-Baki’s candidacy and most discouraged it.

The Council does not publish the straw-poll results, and the ballots are shredded after each poll by a teller appointed among the 15 members. The numbers have nevertheless routinely found their way to journalists and others.

An unwritten Council custom holds that the secretary-general post should rotate among the UN’s regional groups, and this cycle is widely seen as Latin America and the Caribbean’s turn. Six of the current candidates come from the region, but two African nominees are also in contention. It is also considered long time for the UN to be led by a woman, for the first time in its history, yet three men are competing in the race.

Damilola Banjo is an award-winning staff reporter for PassBlue who has covered a wide range of topics, from Africa-centered stories to gender equality to UN peacekeeping and US-UN relations. She also oversees all video production for PassBlue. She was a Dag Hammarskjold fellow in 2023 and a Pulitzer Center postgraduate fellow in 2021. She was part of the BBC Africa team that produced the Emmy-nominated documentary, "Sex for Grades." In addition, she worked for WFAE, an NPR affiliate in Charlotte, N.C. *H.E., Dr. Amb. Olara Otunu the Consensus Figure Late in the Sequence in the 2026 UN Secretary Generalship*

_An expert opinion from Opio J.J. Gregory._

Dr. Olara Otunu joined the UN Secretary Generalship quite late sometime towards the end of July 2026 when his competitors joined the race almost a year ago but this doesn’t substantially erode his chances at all.

Rather than just the tedious but surmountable huddles like on the one hand, the urgent need for him to immediately do backroom alignment amongst the P5 (for starters, P5 means the Permanent Members of the UN Security Council e.g. the US, UK, France, Russia and China) for purposes of avoiding the veto trap by navigating straw polls without early momentum, and on the other, his immediate need to rapidly prove his diplomatic viability under tight scrutiny to avoid member state pushback since he didn’t declare early nor publicly engaged in town halls, make no mistake, Dr. Olara Otunu can still win the UN Secretary Generalship.

I want to believe that he’s going to emerge as a viable compromise candidate because the final choice rests with the P5 especially when there’s likely to be deadlocks over early front-runners hence subsequently paving the way for the late-arriving “dark horse” or fallback candidates like Olara Otunu.

While Dr. Otunu faces compressed timelines for public vetting, intense geopolitical friction among the P5 especially the Gaza issue amongst others like Ukraine and Iran crisis is likely to cause early high-profile favorites to stall and face vetoes very much to their chagrin as Olara Otunu surges forward to SGship victory.

In this likely case when the front runners burn out or trigger a veto, the Security Council shall need to gravitate towards a fresh, widely acceptable consensus figure like Otunu late in the sequence.

The global geopolitics and shifting dynamics is likely to elevate Olara Otunu the late contender, the past late-moving profile if major powers block regional favorites.

And with this, do not be shocked to have H.E., Dr., Amb. Olara Otunu as the shiny, new UN Secretary General in this extraordinary time. The questions on Uganda government sudden U-turn choice and backing of Otunu shall have no bearing whatsoever on the later’s candidature at the global level. They simply remain obnoxious local context domestic political squabbles.
